      <content name="title"><span class="qt3">Depression</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysthymic <span class="qt2">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Clinical <span class="qt3">depression</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt4">depressive</span></span><span class="qt4"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt4">disorder</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Unipolar <span class="qt3">depression</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt3">Depression</span> is more than a feeling of being sad or irritable for a few days. It's a serious mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. As one of the most common mental <span class="qt2">disorders</span> in the United States, <span class="qt3">depression</span> can affect how you think, feel, and your everyday life. You may not know why you feel this way, but even basic daily activities such as sleeping, eating, or working may become difficult. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> often needs long-term treatment but getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage your symptoms.</p>What are the different types of <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>The most common types of <span class="qt3">depression</span> are <span class="qt0">major</span> <span class="qt3">depression</span> and persistent <span class="qt1"><span class="qt4">depressive</span></span><span class="qt4"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt4">disorder</span></span>.</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt3">depression</span> symptoms include a depressed mood or a loss of interest. Symptoms affect your daily activities and last for at least two weeks.</li><li>Persistent <span class="qt1"><span class="qt4">depressive</span></span><span class="qt4"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt4">disorder</span></span> (also called dysthymia or dysthymic <span class="qt2">disorder</span>) has less severe <span class="qt1">depressive</span> symptoms, but they last longer, usually for at least two years.</li></ul><p>Other types of <span class="qt3">depression</span> can include:</p><ul><li>Seasonal affective <span class="qt2">disorder</span> comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer.</li><li>Bipolar <span class="qt2">disorder</span> is sometimes called manic <span class="qt3">depression</span>. This mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span> can cause intense mood swings.</li><li><span class="qt3">Depression</span> with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form of <span class="qt3">depression</span> that also has delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling something that isn't there).</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>There are a variety of things that may cause <span class="qt3">depression</span>, including genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> can happen at any age and can affect anyone, but it's more common in women. This is often due to the physical and hormonal changes that women have during menstruation, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and menopause. Other mental <span class="qt2">disorders</span> or chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or heart disease may occur with <span class="qt3">depression</span>. This may make the chronic condition or <span class="qt3">depression</span> worse.</p><p>In some cases, there is no clear cause for <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</p>Who is at risk of <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>You may be at a higher risk of <span class="qt3">depression</span> if you have a close relative who has it or another mental health <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise your risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt3">Depression</span> doesn't look the same on everyone. The type and number of symptoms of <span class="qt3">depression</span> can vary and don't always appear like sadness. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> may affect you differently based on your:</p><ul><li>Age. The symptoms of <span class="qt3">depression</span> may be different in a child, who may appear more irritable than sad. Teens may act out or have excessive sleepiness. The symptoms for an older adult may not be as obvious as other age groups.</li><li>Sex. Men often show symptoms and coping behaviors differently than women. Rather than sad, men may appear angry or irritable.</li><li>Medical conditions. Some medicines and medical conditions may cause symptoms that look like <span class="qt3">depression</span>. Chronic conditions may make <span class="qt3">depression</span> worse.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of <span class="qt3">depression</span> are ongoing and affect your day-to-day life. They can include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or "empty"</li><li>Losing interest in favorite activities</li><li>Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all</li><li>Sleeping too much, or not enough</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty</li><li>Having aches and pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems</li><li>Having thoughts of death or suicide</li><li>Changing moods or behaviors</li><li>Increasing use of alcohol or drugs</li><li>Isolating from family and friends</li></ul>How is <span class="qt3">depression</span> diagnosed?<p>If you think you have <span class="qt3">depression</span>, talk to your health care provider or a mental health provider. To be diagnosed with <span class="qt3">depression</span>, your provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A medical history will include asking about your symptoms and family history. To be diagnosed with <span class="qt3">depression</span>, your symptoms must occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. One of the symptoms must be a depressed mood or a loss of interest in most activities.</li><li>Medical tests may be done to rule out other medical conditions. Certain medicines and medical conditions (such as viruses or thyroid <span class="qt2">disorders</span>) may cause symptoms like <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</li><li>A physical exam to make sure another issue isn't causing your symptoms.</li><li>A mental health evaluation by your provider or a mental health provider.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt3">Depression</span> may need long-term treatment. Most treatments include medicines and/or psychotherapy (talk therapy):</p><ul><li>Medicines such as antidepressants may help control your symptoms. You may need to try several medicines to find which works best for you. Medicine may take time to work and can have side effects. Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking with your provider. Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicine.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) under the care of a mental health provider can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. This may be done one-on-one or in a group setting. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies.</li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective <span class="qt2">disorder</span> (SAD).</li><li>Other treatments options may be considered if treatment isn't working or if <span class="qt3">depression</span> is severe. These may include:
	<ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses a mild electric current when you are under general anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe <span class="qt3">depression</span> that is not getting better with other treatments.</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve <span class="qt3">depression</span>. It's not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Can <span class="qt3">depression</span> be prevented?<p>Most cases of <span class="qt3">depression</span> can't be prevented, but healthy lifestyle changes can have long-term benefits for your mental health. These can include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular exercise</li><li>Having a consistent sleep schedule</li><li>Controlling stress</li></ul><p>If you, or someone you love is depressed, see your provider or a mental health provider. It's important to get treatment at the earliest sign of a problem.</p><p>If you or someone you know has thoughts of hurting themselves or attempting suicide, get help right away. If it is an emergency, dial 911.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

      <content name="title">Seasonal Affective <span class="qt2">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SAD</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt4">depressive</span></span><span class="qt4"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt4">disorder</span></span> with seasonal pattern</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal <span class="qt3">depression</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Seasonal affective <span class="qt2">disorder</span> (SAD) is a type of <span class="qt3">depression</span> that comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in the late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer. Some people do have episodes of <span class="qt3">depression</span> that start in the spring or summer, but that is a lot less common. Symptoms of SAD may include:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Gloomy outlook</li><li>Feeling hopeless, worthless, and irritable</li><li>Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy</li><li>Low energy</li><li>Difficulty sleeping or oversleeping</li><li>Carbohydrate cravings and weight gain</li><li>Thoughts of death or suicide</li></ul><p>SAD is more common in women, young people, and those who live far from the equator. You are also more likely to have SAD if you or your family members have <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</p><p>The exact causes of SAD are unknown. Researchers have found that people with SAD may have an imbalance of serotonin, a brain chemical that affects your mood. Their bodies also make too much melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep, and not enough vitamin D.</p><p>The main treatment for SAD is light therapy. The idea behind light therapy is to replace the sunshine that you miss during the fall and winter months. You sit in front of a light therapy box every morning to get daily exposure to bright, artificial light. But some people with SAD do not respond to light therapy alone. Antidepressant medicines and talk therapy can reduce SAD symptoms, either alone or combined with light therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/postpartumdepression.html">
      <content name="title">Postpartum <span class="qt3">Depression</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Baby Blues</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Post-pregnancy <span class="qt3">depression</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>Having a baby can be exciting, but it can also be stressful and bring many strong emotions. During the postpartum period, which is the time after you give birth, you may have mood swings, crying spells, or feel anxious. These feelings are common and are often called the postpartum "baby blues". The baby blues usually go away within a few days to a week.</p><p>If your symptoms are more severe and last longer than two weeks, you may have postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</p><p>Postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> is a common but serious mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span> that can begin anytime within the first year after childbirth. Without treatment, symptoms may make it hard to care for your baby or manage daily tasks.</p>What causes postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>The exact cause is unknown, but postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> likely results from a combination of factors, including:</p><ul><li>Sudden changes in hormone levels after pregnancy</li><li>Physical changes, such as dropping thyroid hormone levels</li><li>Lifestyle factors, such as fatigue, lack of sleep, limited support, or recent stressful events</li></ul>Who is at risk for postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>Anyone can develop postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> after childbirth. You might be at higher risk if you:</p><ul><li>Have a history of <span class="qt3">depression</span>, bipolar <span class="qt2">disorder</span>, or a family health history of these conditions</li><li>Had a multiple birth (twins, triplets, or more)</li><li>Gave birth while in your teens</li><li>Had health problems during pregnancy</li><li>Had preterm labor or other complications during childbirth</li><li>Have a baby with special needs</li><li>Have ever experienced domestic violence</li><li>Are dealing with financial stress</li><li>Had an unplanned pregnancy</li></ul>What are the symptoms of postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>Postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> symptoms are more intense and last longer than the baby blues.</p><p>Symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or empty most of the time</li><li>Eating too much or too little</li><li>Sleeping too much or too little</li><li>Crying more than usual or for no clear reason</li><li>Feeling unusually angry</li><li>Pulling away from family and friends</li><li>Feeling worried or anxious often</li><li>Feeling little or no interest in your baby</li><li>Constant doubts about your ability to care for your baby</li><li>Thinking of harming yourself or your baby</li></ul><p>If you have thoughts about suicide, or hurting yourself or your baby get help right away:</p><ul><li>Call 911 or go to your local emergency room</li><li>Contact a crisis hotline. In the United States, you can reach the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at any time:
	<ul><li>Call or text 988</li><li>Chat online with Lifeline Chat</li><li>TTY users: Use your preferred relay service or dial 711 then 988</li></ul>
</li><li>Veterans can contact the Veterans Crisis Line:
	<ul><li>Call 988, then press 1</li><li>Text 838255</li><li>Chat online</li></ul>
</li><li>Call your mental health provider or other health care provider</li><li>Reach out to a loved one or close friend</li></ul><p>If these symptoms begin during pregnancy and continue after childbirth, it's called perinatal <span class="qt3">depression</span>. Without treatment, it can affect bonding with your baby and may contribute to feeding or sleeping problems.</p><p>Very rarely, a new mother may develop postpartum psychosis, a medical emergency. Symptoms may include confusion, hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that aren't real), or dangerous behaviors. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room right away if this happens.</p>How is postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> diagnosed?<p>Your provider may diagnose postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> using:</p><ul><li>Screening questions or questionnaires, such as those about your mood, sleep, and thoughts.</li><li>A clinical evaluation based on your symptoms.</li><li>Blood tests, if needed, to check for physical conditions such as thyroid <span class="qt2">disorders</span>, that can cause or worsen <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</li></ul>What is the treatment for postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p>If you think you have postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span>, talk with your provider. Treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Medicines, including antidepressants</li><li>Talk therapy (counseling)</li></ul><p>Tell your provider if you are breastfeeding so they can choose the safest treatment options.</p><p>Along with these treatment options, there are things you can do at home that may help you feel better, such as:</p><ul><li>Asking for help with caring for the baby and household chores</li><li>Taking time for yourself</li><li>Getting physical activity, such as walking</li><li>Resting when the baby rests</li></ul>Can postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> be prevented?<p>You may be able to lower your risk for postpartum <span class="qt3">depression</span> by:</p><ul><li>Talking with your provider during pregnancy about any history of <span class="qt3">depression</span></li><li>Completing recommended screening questionnaires during pregnancy and after birth</li><li>Getting support from family, friends, or support groups</li><li>Attending early Physical changes so symptoms can be found and treated as soon as possible</li></ul><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/teendepression.html">
      <content name="title">Teen <span class="qt3">Depression</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Depression</span>, Teen</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens?<p><span class="qt3">Depression</span> in teens (ages 13-17) is a serious medical illness. It's more than just a feeling of being sad or "blue" for a few days. It is an intense feeling of sadness, hopelessness, and anger or frustration that lasts much longer. These feelings make it hard for you to function normally and do your usual activities. You may also have trouble focusing and have no motivation or energy. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> can make you feel like it is hard to enjoy life or even get through the day.</p>What causes <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens?<p>Many factors may play a role in <span class="qt3">depression</span>, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> can run in families.</li><li>Brain biology and chemistry.</li><li>Hormones. Hormone changes can contribute to <span class="qt3">depression</span>.</li><li>Stressful childhood events such as trauma, the death of a loved one, bullying, and abuse.</li></ul>Which teens are at risk of <span class="qt3">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt3">Depression</span> can happen at any age, but often begins in the teens or early adulthood. Certain teens are at higher risk of <span class="qt3">depression</span>, such as those who:</p><ul><li>Have other mental health conditions, such as anxiety, eating <span class="qt2">disorders</span>, and substance use</li><li>Have other diseases, such as diabetes, cancer, and heart disease</li><li>Have family members with mental illness</li><li>Have a dysfunctional family/family conflict</li><li>Have problems with friends or other kids at school</li><li>Have learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity <span class="qt2">disorder (ADHD</span>)</li><li>Have had trauma in childhood</li><li>Have low self-esteem, a pessimistic outlook, or poor coping skills</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens?<p>If you have <span class="qt3">depression</span>, you have one or more of these symptoms most of the time:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Feeling of emptiness</li><li>Hopelessness</li><li>Being angry, irritable, or frustrated, even at minor things</li></ul><p>You also may also have other symptoms, such as:</p><ul><li>No longer caring about things you used to enjoy</li><li>Changes in weight, such as losing weight when you are not dieting or gaining weight from eating too much</li><li>Changes in sleep, such as having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual</li><li>Feeling restless or having trouble sitting still</li><li>Feeling very tired or not having energy</li><li>Feeling worthless or very guilty</li><li>Having trouble concentrating, remembering information, or making decisions</li><li>Thinking about dying or suicide</li></ul>How is <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens diagnosed?<p>If you think you might be depressed, tell someone that you trust, such as your:</p><ul><li>Parents or guardian</li><li>Teacher or counselor</li><li>Doctor</li></ul><p>The next step is to see your doctor for a checkup. Your doctor can first make sure that you do not have another health problem that is causing your <span class="qt3">depression</span>. To do this, you may have a physical exam and lab tests.</p><p>If you don't have another health problem, you will get a psychological evaluation. Your doctor may do it, or you may be referred to a mental health professional to get one. You may be asked about things such as:</p><ul><li>Your thoughts and feelings</li><li>How you are doing at school</li><li>Any changes in your eating, sleeping, or energy level</li><li>Whether you are suicidal</li><li>Whether you use alcohol or drugs</li></ul>How is <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens treated?<p>Effective treatments for <span class="qt3">depression</span> in teens include talk therapy, or a combination of talk therapy and medicines:</p><p>Talk therapy</p><p>Talk therapy, also called psychotherapy or counseling, can help you understand and manage your moods and feelings. It involves going to see a therapist, such as a psychiatrist, a psychologist, a social worker, or counselor. You can talk out your emotions to someone who understands and supports you. You can also learn how to stop thinking negatively and start to look at the positives in life. This will help you build confidence and feel better about yourself.</p><p>There are many different types of talk therapy. Certain types have been shown to help teens deal with <span class="qt3">depression</span>, including:</p><ul><li>Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps you to identify and change negative and unhelpful thoughts. It also helps you build coping skills and change behavioral patterns.</li><li>Interpersonal therapy (IPT), which focuses on improving your relationships. It helps you understand and work through troubled relationships that may contribute to your <span class="qt3">depression</span>. IPT may help you change behaviors that are causing problems.  You also explore <span class="qt0">major</span> issues that may add to your <span class="qt3">depression</span>, such as grief or life changes.</li></ul><p>Medicines</p><p>In some cases, your doctor will suggest medicines along with talk therapy. There are a few antidepressants that have been widely studied and proven to help teens. If you are taking medicine for <span class="qt3">depression</span>, it is important to see your doctor regularly.</p><p>It is also important to know that it will take some time for you to get relief from antidepressants:</p><ul><li>It can take 3 to 4 weeks until an antidepressant takes effect</li><li>You may have to try more than one antidepressant to find one that works for you</li><li>It can also take some time to find the right dose of an antidepressant</li></ul><p>In some cases, teenagers may have an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior when taking antidepressants. This risk is higher in the first few weeks after starting the medicine and when the dose is changed. Make sure to tell your parents or guardian if you start feeling worse or have thoughts of hurting yourself.</p><p>You should not stop taking the antidepressants on your own. You need to work with your doctor to slowly and safely decrease the dose before you stop.</p><p>Programs for severe <span class="qt3">depression</span></p><p>Some teens who have severe <span class="qt3">depression</span> or are at risk of hurting themselves may need more intensive treatment. They may go into a psychiatric hospital or do a day program. Both offer counseling, group discussions, and activities with mental health professionals and other patients. Day programs may be full-day or half-day, and they often last for several weeks.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/antidepressants.html">
      <content name="title">Antidepressants</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Atypical Antidepressants</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SNRIs </content>
      <content name="altTitle">SSRIs</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Serotonin and Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Depression</span> Medicines</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are antidepressants?<p>Antidepressants are prescription medicines to treat <span class="qt3">depression. Depression</span> is more than feeling a little sad or "blue" for a few days. It's a very common, serious medical illness that affects your mood and general mental health. It can make you feel tired, hopeless, worried, or fearful. It can change your thinking, sleeping, and eating. <span class="qt3">Depression</span> may make some people think about ending their lives.</p><p>But antidepressants can help many people who have <span class="qt3">depression</span>. Researchers think antidepressants may help improve the way your brain uses certain chemicals that control mood or stress.</p>Are antidepressants used for other conditions?<p>A health care provider may prescribe antidepressants for anxiety, chronic pain, or insomnia. Sometimes providers also prescribe antidepressants for other conditions.</p>What are the different types of antidepressants?<p>There are many types of antidepressants. Each one works differently. Providers usually prescribe newer antidepressants first because they don't cause as many side effects as older types. They also seem to help more kinds of <span class="qt3">depression</span> and anxiety problems.</p><p>Most of the newer antidepressants belong to one of these three groups:</p><ul><li>Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)</li><li>Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)</li><li>Atypical antidepressants, which are newer antidepressants that don't fit into the other groups</li></ul><p>If these antidepressants don't help, your provider might suggest one of the older antidepressants. The older types include tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), tetracyclics, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). Even though these antidepressants may cause more serious side effects, the benefits may outweigh the risks for some people.</p>Which type of antidepressant is right for me?<p>Our bodies and brains all work differently. That means one antidepressant won't work for everyone.  You may need to try two or more medicines before you find one that works for you.</p><p>Your provider will work with you to choose the best option to try first. You'll consider questions such as:</p><ul><li>Which symptoms bother you most? Some antidepressants may do a better job helping specific symptoms, such as trouble sleeping.</li><li>What other medicines and supplements do you take? Some antidepressants can cause problems if you take them with certain medicines and herbs.</li><li>Did a certain antidepressant work well for a close relative? An antidepressant that helped a parent, brother, or sister could be a good choice for you, too.</li><li>Do you have other health conditions? Certain antidepressants can make some other conditions better or worse. Any other conditions that you have will be part of choosing your <span class="qt3">depression</span> treatment.</li><li>Are you pregnant, planning for pregnancy, or breastfeeding?  If so, your provider will help you find a way to treat your <span class="qt3">depression</span> that's safe for you and your baby.</li></ul>How long do antidepressants take to work?<p>Antidepressants usually take 4 to 8 weeks to work, so you'll need to be patient. You may notice that some problems, such as sleeping and eating, get better before your mood improves. That's a good sign. You may just need to give the medicine a little more time to do its job.</p><p>Sometimes an antidepressant helps at first, but symptoms return while you're still taking it. But there's usually another one you can try. To get more relief from <span class="qt3">depression</span>, your provider may suggest combining two antidepressants, using another kind of medicine with an antidepressant, or adding talk therapy or other approaches to improve your mental health.</p>How long will I need to take an antidepressant?<p>When an antidepressant starts to work, you and your provider can decide how long you need to stay on it. The typical length of treatment is 6 to 12 months, but some people may stay on antidepressants for much longer.</p>What are the side effects of antidepressants?<p>Not everyone has side effects from antidepressants. But if you do have them, they're usually mild and may get better over time as your body gets used to the new medicine.</p><p>The most common side effects from antidepressants include:</p><ul><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Weight gain</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Sleepiness</li><li>Sexual problems, such as a lack of desire or ability to have sex</li></ul><p>When thinking about side effects, it's important to remember that there are also risks from not treating <span class="qt3">depression</span>. Your provider can help you think through the pros and cons of all your options.</p><p>If you have any side effects from antidepressants, your provider may suggest ways to manage them while you wait to see if the antidepressant will work. If the side effects bother you too much, you may need to change antidepressants. But you should never change your dose or stop taking an antidepressant on your own.</p><p>If you have serious problems or notice any changes that worry you, such as new or worsening symptoms, unusual changes in your mood, or you start acting differently, call your provider right away.</p><p>In some cases, children, teenagers, and young adults under 25 may be more likely to think about hurting or killing themselves when starting antidepressants or when the dose is changed. Get medical help right away if this happens.</p>What can I do to take antidepressants safely?<p>Antidepressants are generally safe when you use them correctly:</p><ul><li>Tell your provider about everything you take. That includes medicines, herbs, supplements, and over-the-counter medicines you take, such as pain relievers and decongestants. Be honest about recreational drugs and alcohol, too.</li><li>Try to get all your medicines from the same pharmacy. That way the pharmacist can warn you and your provider if you take medicines that may cause problems when used together.</li><li>Follow all instructions about how to take your medicine.</li><li>Talk with your provider if side effects bother you.</li><li>Never stop taking antidepressants without your provider's help. Stopping too fast may make <span class="qt3">depression</span> come back. You could even make your condition worse. To stop antidepressants safely, you need to give your body time to get used to being without the medicine. Your provider can tell you the safest way to go off an antidepressant.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>
